segments.say: Lesson 5. Load Balancers. L4 versus L7, algorithms (round robin, least connections, consistent hash), health checks and sticky sessions.

A load balancer sits in front of many servers and spreads incoming requests across them, skipping any server that is unhealthy. Here is an analogy. The receptionist at a busy clinic sending each patient to whichever doctor is free, and never to a doctor who has gone home sick.

Why does this matter? Needed as soon as you have more than one server, which is every design. A few key words. Round robin: Take turns: A, B, C, A. Least connections: Send to the least busy server. Health check: Regular "are you alive?" ping. L4 / L7: Routes by I P/port versus understands H T T P paths. Sticky session: Pin a user to one server (usually avoid).
Load balancing algorithms. A load balancer spreads requests across healthy servers. It also gives you a single entry point.
Round robin: A leads to B leads to C leads to A. Simple, good when servers and requests are similar.
. B next. But B is already busy with 9 slow connections. Round robin doesn't know.
Least connections: send to the server with the fewest active connections (C). Better for uneven request durations, like websockets.
Weighted variants give bigger servers more traffic. I P / consistent hashing sends the same client or key to the same server (cache affinity).
Health checks: B fails /health, so the L B stops routing to it until it recovers. That's automatic failover.

L4 versus L7. L4 (transport): routes by I P and port with T C P/U D P. Very fast, protocol-agnostic, can't see U R Ls. L7 (application): understands H T T P: routes by path or header ( /api leads to A P I pool, /img leads to media), T L S termination, auth, rate limiting, caching. Slightly more overhead.

Practical concerns. The L B is itself a single point of failure? Run it redundantly (active-passive or managed: A W S A L B/N L B, G C P L B), plus D N S-level balancing across regions. Sticky sessions: pin a user to a server. Avoid it, because it breaks even load distribution and failover. Prefer stateless servers. Connection draining during deploys. Global server load balancing (GeoDNS / anycast) across regions.

Say it in the interview. "I'd use a managed L7 load balancer for T L S termination and path-based routing, least-connections for uneven request times, active health checks for failover, and no sticky sessions because servers are stateless. Across regions, GeoDNS or anycast in front.".

Let's compare. Round robin: rotate in order, uniform servers & requests. Weighted R R: rotate by capacity, mixed server sizes. Least connections: fewest active conns, long or uneven requests. Least response time: fastest plus fewest, latency-sensitive. I P hash / consistent hash: hash(client or key) leads to server, cache affinity, sticky routing.

L4 versus L7. Sees: I P, port, H T T P path, headers, cookies. Speed: fastest, slightly slower. Features: basic routing, T L S, path routing, auth, W A F. Example: A W S N L B, A W S A L B, N G I N X, Envoy.

A likely interview question: L4 versus L7 load balancer? A strong answer: L4 routes on I P and port (fast, protocol-agnostic). L7 understands H T T P, so it can route by path or header, terminate T L S, and do auth, rate limiting and caching.
That's it for Load Balancers. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
